status: Editorial teaching dependency map; teacher review remains possible. Not official IB prerequisite rules.
entryAssumptions: Basic numeracy, graph reading and common laboratory language are assumed. S1.1.1 is a descriptive entry point; detailed bond models are taught later.

sources.title: Existing guide transcription and source record

nodes.reason: Entry point: identify elements, compounds and mixtures descriptively before explaining their microscopic structure.
States and changes of state refer to the substances and mixtures already identified.
Interpret temperature through the moving-particle model of matter.
Introduce internal atomic structure after identifying elements as types of atoms.
Isotopes require proton and neutron counts and elemental identity.
Interpret isotope peaks and abundance-weighted relative atomic masses.
Electronic emission needs electrons, nuclei and excitation/relaxation between energy states.
Interpret the hydrogen line spectrum using the emission model.
Electron shell capacity builds on the nuclear/electron model; spectral inference is a parallel route.
Sublevels refine the shell/energy-level model.
Orbital occupancy and spin refine subshell structure.
Relate spectral convergence to removal of an electron and formation of an ion.
Successive electron removal is interpreted using configurations, occupied shells and ion formation.
Counting particles by amount requires identifying the chemical entities being counted.
Relative atomic masses and the carbon-12 reference require isotope identity.
Connect amount of substance to relative atomic/formula masses and mass per mole.
Determine simplest atom ratios and connect empirical and molecular formulas using molar masses.
Concentration relates amount of dissolved entities to solution volume.
Compare gas particle counts and volumes at controlled temperature and pressure.
Ideal gases refine the moving-particle model and its temperature dependence.
Explain departures from ideality using finite particle volume and intermolecular attractions.
Molar gas volume connects the ideal model to particle counts and amounts.
Use quantitative relationships between gas amount, temperature, pressure and volume.
Ion formation requires outer-shell electrons, electron counts and main-group valence patterns.
Electrostatic attraction requires identifying oppositely charged ions.
Extend ionic attractions into lattices and express their ratios as empirical formulas.
Shared electron pairs and octets build on valence shells and electron counts.
Distinguish one, two and three shared bonding pairs.
Coordinate bonds require the shared-electron-pair model and lone-pair donation.
Draw bonding/lone-pair domains and distinguish bond multiplicity before predicting shapes.
Unequal electron sharing requires covalent bonding and periodic electronegativity trends.
Molecular polarity combines bond dipoles with three-dimensional geometry.
Network structures extend covalent bonding beyond discrete molecules.
Intermolecular attractions require particle size, electron distributions and molecular polarity.
Compare physical properties with attention to both interactions and comparable molar mass.
Separation of mixtures depends on competing attractions to mobile and stationary phases.
Resonance requires alternative valid Lewis connectivities of electron pairs and multiple bonds.
Apply resonance to the ring structure and formula representations of benzene.
Expanded-octet species extend electron counting and domain-based shape prediction.
Evaluate Lewis alternatives by assigning formal charges and conserving total ionic charge.
Sigma/pi bonding combines atomic orbital shapes with single and multiple covalent bonds.
Hybrid orbitals connect orbital overlap to spatial arrangements and sigma/pi bonding.
Metallic bonding requires cations, electron loss and mobile delocalised electrons.
Metallic bond strength depends on ion charge and periodic variation in ion size.
Extend metallic delocalisation to d electrons with an orbital occupancy model.
The continuum compares the ionic, covalent and metallic bonding models.
Locate substances in the bonding triangle using bonding character and electronegativity.
Explain alloy properties through metallic structure modified by mixing constituents.
Monomers and polymer chains require molecular structural representations and covalent connectivity.
Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers by changing double-bond connectivity.
Condensation polymers require reacting functional groups and accounting for the eliminated molecule.
Periodic classification uses atomic number and elemental identity.
Connect periods/groups with occupied shells and valence electrons.
Explain periodic trends using nuclear attraction, shielding and outer-shell structure.
Group reactivity trends connect periodic properties with electron loss and gain.
Metallic character and oxide acidity/basicity require periodic trends and neutralisation concepts.
Assign oxidation states using ionic charge and electronegativity-based electron assignment.
Explain exceptions to ionisation trends using subshell occupancy, spin and successive-removal reasoning.
Transition-element properties require incomplete d subshells and the configurations of atoms/ions.
Variable oxidation states connect transition-electron occupancy with ionisation energies and electron counting.
Explain colour using metal-ion d occupancy, ligand coordination and absorption-driven electronic transitions.
Organic representations require molecular formulas, covalent connectivity and bond multiplicity.
Recognise characteristic groups within structural and skeletal representations.
Group compounds into homologous families using functional groups and repeating composition changes.
Homologous physical-property trends combine changing molecular size with intermolecular forces.
Systematic names express carbon skeletons, functional groups and homologous-family membership.
Distinguish identical molecular formulas with different connectivity by drawing/naming structures.
Distinguish connectivity from spatial isomerism using molecular geometry and restricted rotation about pi bonds.
Interpret organic molecular/fragment ions using mass spectra and molecular connectivity.
Interpret bond vibrations and diagnostic functional-group absorptions; bond polarity underpins IR activity.
Proton NMR requires nuclear/isotope identity, functional groups and chemical environments affected by electron shielding.
Apply neighbouring-hydrogen reasoning to already identified NMR environments.
Combine complementary MS, IR and NMR evidence rather than interpreting an unfamiliar technique first.
Define energy transfer between a material system and its surroundings.
Relate the direction of energy transfer to temperature observations.
Compare energy/stability of reactants and products using endothermic/exothermic change.
Standard molar enthalpy changes require energy transfer, reaction equations and amount of substance.
Relate reaction energetics to the energy needed to break and form covalent bonds.
Hess cycles combine appropriately scaled enthalpy changes under defined conditions.
Define molar formation/combustion data with balanced equations and combustion context.
Calculate cycles from Hess law plus standard formation/combustion data.
Born–Haber cycles combine ionic lattice formation, ionisation and bond/atomisation energy steps.
Describe combustion with balanced equations and energy release.
Compare complete/incomplete combustion of carbon-based molecular fuels.
Evaluate fossil fuels using composition, combustion products and incomplete combustion consequences.
Relate biologically produced molecular fuels to combustion and their functional groups.
Contrast fuel-cell redox energy conversion with direct combustion.
Dispersal of matter/energy requires particle states and a defined system.
Combine entropy, enthalpy and absolute temperature in Gibbs energy.
Apply the sign of Gibbs energy to spontaneity under fixed conditions.
Connect driving force to the approach to dynamic equilibrium.
Balanced reaction equations conserve atoms represented by chemical formulas.
Use coefficients with amount–mass, concentration and gas-volume conversions.
Compare available amounts with reaction mole ratios to identify limiting reactant and theoretical yield.
Compare measured product with the limiting-reactant theoretical yield.
Atom economy requires balanced product allocation and formula/molar masses.
Measure changes in reactant/product concentration with time.
Reaction collisions require moving particles, energy distributions and reacting species.
Explain measured rate changes through collision frequency, temperature, pressure and exposed particles.
Introduce a reaction energy barrier using collision energy and reaction-energy profiles.
Explain catalysis as an alternative lower-barrier pathway that changes rate.
Resolve an overall reaction into elementary steps and identify the rate-determining step.
Construct multistep energy profiles with individual activation barriers and transition states.
Count particles in an elementary step rather than coefficients in an overall equation.
Relate measured concentration dependence to mechanisms without assuming overall stoichiometry gives rate law.
Interpret individual exponents and their sum in an experimentally determined rate law.
Calculate the constant and its units using the established rate equation and overall order.
Relate temperature-dependent rate constants to activation energy on an absolute temperature scale.
Interpret the Arrhenius prefactor through collision frequency and orientation.
Dynamic equilibrium compares forward and reverse reaction rates in a closed system.
Build equilibrium expressions from stoichiometry and equilibrium concentrations.
Interpret the magnitude of the equilibrium constant after constructing its expression.
Predict responses to concentration, pressure and temperature changes using equilibrium and energetic context.
Compare reaction quotient and K using the same expression at different mixture compositions.
Solve equilibrium composition using K, concentrations and reaction amount changes.
Relate equilibrium position/K to Gibbs energy and its equilibrium limit.
Proton transfer requires charged species, lone-pair bond formation and reaction equations.
Identify acid/base partners differing by one transferred proton.
Recognise species able to donate or accept a proton in different conjugate-pair contexts.
Relate solution hydrogen-ion concentration to the logarithmic pH scale.
Treat water ionisation as an equilibrium linking hydrogen- and hydroxide-ion concentrations.
Acid/base strength depends on extent of ionisation, distinct from concentration.
Represent acid/base neutralisation as a proton-transfer reaction with conserved atoms and charge.
Construct strong acid/base titration curves using neutralisation stoichiometry and pH.
Extend logarithmic concentration notation to hydroxide and link pH/pOH through water ionisation.
Quantify weak-acid/base ionisation equilibria using K and logarithmic measures.
Relate conjugate-pair equilibrium constants using the water ion product.
Predict salt-solution pH from conjugate-ion acid/base equilibria.
Extend titration curves to weak-acid/base equilibria and buffer regions.
Treat indicator colour change as a weak-acid conjugate-pair equilibrium shifted by pH.
Choose an indicator by matching its transition interval with the titration equivalence-region pH change.
Explain buffering through a weak acid/base and its conjugate partner responding to added acid/base.
Calculate buffer pH from equilibrium constants and conjugate-pair amount/concentration ratios.
Describe redox using electron transfer and oxidation-state changes in reactions.
Balance separate oxidation/reduction steps conserving charge as well as atoms.
Compare relative oxidation/reduction tendencies using periodic and displacement-reaction patterns.
Explain metal–acid hydrogen formation as redox involving hydrogen ions.
Locate oxidation/reduction half-reactions at anode and cathode.
Connect electrode half-reactions, ion/electron transport and conversion of chemical energy to electrical energy.
Rechargeable cells reverse the redox processes established in a voltaic cell.
Contrast externally driven electrolysis with spontaneous voltaic-cell operation.
Track oxidation changes of recognisable organic functional groups.
Compare functional-group reduction with the corresponding organic oxidation transformations.
Hydrogen addition reduces unsaturation by changing multiple-bond connectivity.
Define a reference hydrogen electrode within an electrochemical-cell and hydrogen-ion context.
Combine reference electrode potentials with the direction of balanced half-reactions.
Relate cell potential and transferred electron amount to Gibbs energy/spontaneity.
Compare competing aqueous electrode reactions using electrolysis and electrode-potential reasoning.
Apply controlled aqueous metal-ion reduction to deposition at a cathode.
Identify unpaired electrons in molecular entities using orbital occupancy and covalent bonding.
Explain equal splitting of a bonding pair and the role of photon/thermal energy in radical generation.
Follow radical chain substitution in recognised alkane structures with balanced transformations.
Electron-pair donation requires lone pairs, coordinate bond formation and electron-rich sites.
Substitution combines nucleophile/electrophile roles, heterolytic bond cleavage and organic connectivity.
Unequal allocation of a covalent bonding pair produces ionic fragments.
Contrast electron-pair acceptance with donation and identify complementary reaction partners.
Recognise alkene multiple-bond electron density as a target for an electron-pair acceptor.
Generalise electron-pair donation/acceptance beyond proton transfer and organic reaction partners.
Apply Lewis donor/acceptor roles to the formation of coordinate covalent bonds.
Ligand donation to transition-metal cations requires coordination bonding and transition-ion electronic structure.
Apply nucleophilic substitution to halogenoalkanes and distinguish possible reaction mechanisms.
Interpret leaving-group effects on measured substitution rates and mechanism.
Develop alkene electrophilic addition mechanisms using pi bonding and heterolytic electron-pair movement.
Compare alternative carbocation intermediates to predict addition pathways and products.
Electrophilic substitution in benzene requires delocalised aromatic pi bonding and electrophile electron-pair acceptance.
